title: Writing Instruction: A Cat With Nine Lives Hanging On By Its Tail in Texas
author: Underwood, Terry
source: Learning to Read, Reading to Learn (Substack)
summary: Terry Underwood traces the fragmented state of writing instruction in Texas through two decades of policy decisions that prioritized machine scoring, reduced the grade levels at which writing was explicitly tested, and ultimately gutted teachers' ability to deliver sustained writing instruction. The article follows the arc of the Texas Education Agency's shift away from multiple-choice assessments toward constructed-response items, a reform that raised legitimate hopes among writing teachers—then dashed them when machine scoring was introduced to handle the resulting volume. Underwood argues that machine-scored writing assessment punishes authentic voice, syntactic complexity, and the very features of mature writing that human teachers cultivate. The piece is anchored in teacher testimony (particularly seventh-grade teacher Erika De La Rosa) and literacy research, making the case that writing instruction at scale is still being treated as a logistical problem rather than a pedagogical one.
points: Grade-level targeting of writing tests creates a pernicious instructional gap: when writing is only tested in grades 4 and 7, teachers in intervening grades abandon explicit writing instruction entirely.

Machine scoring penalizes sophisticated writing: features valued by human readers—unusual vocabulary, syntactic complexity, emotional authenticity—are penalized by machine scoring algorithms that optimize for readability formulas.

The shift to constructed response raised hope then delivered betrayal: teachers saw potential for restoring writing instruction when multiple-choice was deemphasized, but machine scoring erased the benefit.

Writing instruction is a social contract that the system is breaking: when schools fail to develop students as writers, they transfer the cost to the students who then enter higher education and workplaces unprepared.
The solution is not more assessment but sustained, expert writing instruction across all grade levels—something the current testing and scoring infrastructure actively discourages.
quotes: What I saw for years was that because it was only tested in fourth and seventh grade, students would only get explicit writing instruction in fourth and seventh grade.

As a seventh-grade teacher, I would be scrambling to try to figure out how can I cover all of these grammar mechanics? How do I cover all of these writing techniques? What can I drop? What do we need to focus on?

Legislation early in the 2020s required TEA to reduce its reliance on multiple-choice items in favor of constructed-response items. Researchers in writing assessment have long documented the unfortunate consequences of grade-level targeting of writing.

Erika De La Rosa was right to hope. She was right to be disappointed. The obligation now is to keep saying clearly what is being lost before the generation that never learned to write inherits the consequences.
Everything we know about how human beings develop as thinkers through language is at stake in these decisions about writing instruction and assessment.
